echoes.note: Jesus' first reply (v.4) quotes verbatim 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.' High Volume (explicit 'It is written' + near-exact wording) and Thematic Coherence: Deut 8:3 interprets the wilderness manna as God's pedagogy to teach Israel dependence on his word; Jesus, fasting in the wilderness, recapitulates and passes the test Israel failed.

Jesus' second reply (v.7) quotes 'You shall not test the LORD your God.' Formula 'it is written' + verbatim citation. In Deut 6:16 the warning is 'as you tested him at Massah' (water from the rock); Jesus refuses to coerce God's protective care, again reversing Israel's wilderness failure.

Jesus' climactic reply (v.10) 'You shall worship the LORD your God, and you shall serve him only' quotes Deut 6:13 (LXX adds 'only/alone'). High Volume formula citation; the demand for exclusive worship answers Satan's demand to be worshiped (v.9).

Satan's temptation (v.6) quotes verbatim 'He will command his angels concerning you... on their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.' Verbatim citation with formula 'it is written' — Scripture cited by the tempter, demonstrating the contest is over interpretation, not knowledge.

The forty days and forty nights of fasting (v.2) echoes Moses' forty days and nights on Sinai without bread or water (Exod 34:28; also Exod 24:18). Strong verbal and numeric match; the new-Moses typology recurs throughout Matthew (mountain, law-giver).

Moses 'neither ate bread nor drank water forty days and forty nights' (Deut 9:9, 18) parallels Jesus' fast; Matthew's Deuteronomic quotation chain makes this Deuteronomy theophany-fast a likely background to the forty-day frame.

Israel's forty years of wilderness wandering/testing (a year for each day of spying) stands behind Jesus' forty days. Hays' Thematic Coherence: each of Jesus' three answers is drawn from Deut's reflection on those forty years (manna, Massah, idolatry), framing Jesus as faithful Israel reduced to one obedient Son.

The manna 'test' ('that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law') underlies the bread temptation; Deut 8:3 (quoted) is the interpretive lens, but Exod 16's hunger-and-bread test is the recurrent narrative source.

Massah/Meribah, where Israel 'tested the LORD' demanding water — the very event Deut 6:16 names — supplies the recurrent background for the temple-pinnacle scene where Jesus refuses to put God to the test.

'The LORD led you these forty years in the wilderness... testing you to know what was in your heart.' Verbal kinship with v.1 ('led up... into the wilderness to be tempted') and the whole framing of a divinely-led wilderness test.

'As a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you' — the father/son wilderness-discipline theme resonates with the repeated 'If you are the Son of God' challenge framing Jesus' wilderness testing.

'Israel is my firstborn son' — the divine-sonship of Israel that Jesus recapitulates; Satan's taunt 'If you are the Son of God' presses on the sonship just declared at the baptism (3:17) and rooted in Israel's corporate sonship.

The tempter ('serpent'/devil) offers food and god-like status; Eve's threefold desire (good for food, delight to eyes, to make wise) loosely patterns the three temptations (bread, spectacle, kingdoms). Adam typology: where the first man fell, Jesus stands. Disputed in detail, hence contested.
'The Satan' (the adversary) granted access to test a righteous man under divine permission parallels the devil's testing role; the title 'Satan' Jesus uses (v.10) draws on this adversary figure.

From a high mountain Moses is shown all the land/kingdoms; the devil takes Jesus to 'an exceedingly high mountain' and shows him all the kingdoms of the world (v.8). The Moses-on-Pisgah panorama is inverted — a counterfeit Nebo offering the world by idolatry rather than promise.
The demand for undivided allegiance ('serve him only', v.10) recalls the Deuteronomic monotheism dramatized at Carmel; faint thematic recurrence of 'serve the LORD alone.'

The Father gives the Son 'the nations as your heritage'; Satan counterfeits this by offering 'all the kingdoms of the world' (v.8-9) on his own terms. Royal-Son enthronement (cf. 3:17 'my Son') makes the kingdoms-offer a parody of Ps 2's promised dominion.
Universal dominion over 'all peoples, nations' given to the Son of Man — the legitimate eschatological kingship the devil offers as a shortcut without the cross. Faint, thematic.
Elijah in the wilderness, fed by an angel, journeys forty days; angels minister to Jesus after his forty-day wilderness fast (v.11). Recurrent prophet-in-wilderness, angelically-sustained pattern.

The verse immediately after Satan's quotation ('you will tread on the lion and the adder') promises mastery over the adversary — an ironic uncited remainder of Ps 91 that the narrative enacts as Jesus masters the devil.
'The LORD rebuke you, Satan!' — the heavenly rebuke of the accuser resonates with Jesus' 'Get behind me, Satan!' (v.10). Faint verbal/thematic recurrence of rebuking the adversary.
The Shema's command to love/serve God with whole heart frames the cluster of Deut 6 citations; exclusive devotion to the one LORD is the theological center of Jesus' resistance.

vv.15-16 quote Isa 9:1-2 with formula 'that it might be fulfilled... through Isaiah': 'land of Zebulun and Naphtali... Galilee of the Gentiles, the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.' High Volume formula citation; Matthew geographically anchors Jesus' Galilean ministry in Isaiah's promise of light to the despised northern tribes first to suffer Assyrian conquest.

The immediately preceding context of the quotation — 'gloom of anguish... region and shadow of death' — supplies the contrast of darkness the 'great light' dispels; Matthew's citation spans the Isa 8/9 seam.
Tiglath-pileser's deportation of Zebulun/Naphtali (Galilee) sets the historical 'darkness' Isa 9 reverses; the named tribes carry this exile memory. Background, faint.

'Arise, shine, for your light has come... nations shall come to your light' — recurrent Isaianic light-to-the-nations theme reinforcing 'Galilee of the Gentiles' seeing the light. Thematic, contested as a distinct source.
The servant given 'as a light to the nations, to open eyes that are blind' resonates with Jesus as the light dawning on Gentile Galilee. Faint thematic recurrence.

'Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand' (v.17) opens with the prophetic call to repentance characteristic of Jonah/the prophets; Matthew later pairs Jonah-Nineveh with repentance preaching (12:41). Faint, generic prophetic echo.
'Repent and turn... why will you die?' — the prophetic summons to repentance underlies Jesus' inaugural proclamation. Generic, contested.

'The God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed' grounds 'the Kingdom of Heaven' (v.17); Matthew's signature 'Kingdom of Heaven' reflects Danielic heaven-kingdom expectation. Thematic, recurrent.

Elijah's call of Elisha — who is plowing, leaves his oxen, and immediately follows — patterns the immediate abandonment of nets/boat/father by the fishermen (vv.20, 22). Strong narrative parallel of prophetic call met by instant, total following.

'I will send for many fishers, says the LORD, and they shall fish them' — the prophetic 'fishers' image stands behind 'I will make you fishers for men' (v.19). Verbal borrowing of the fishing-for-people metaphor, though Jeremiah's is judgment and Jesus' is gathering.
Fishermen spreading nets at the life-giving river/sea of the eschatological temple vision; faint resonance with calling fishermen into kingdom-mission abundance.

'He will take you away with hooks, the last of you with fishhooks' — another prophetic fishing-as-gathering image contributing to the recurrent metaphor behind 'fishers for men.' Faint, judgment-toned.
Humanity caught 'like fish of the sea... they bring them up with a net' — recurrent OT trope of people-as-fish-in-nets resonant with the fishing-for-men commission. Contested.

Jesus 'healing every disease and every sickness' (v.23-24) enacts the Isaianic restoration where 'the eyes of the blind shall be opened... the lame leap'; Matthew elsewhere makes this explicit (11:5). Thematic Coherence with the in-breaking kingdom.
'He bore our sicknesses' — the healing summary anticipates Matthew's own citation of Isa 53:4 over the healings in 8:17, making this servant-healing theology a likely background here too.
'Who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases' — the divine prerogative to heal 'all diseases' is exercised by Jesus, a faint resonance of God's healing kingship.
'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings' — eschatological dawning healing connects to the 'light dawned' (v.16) now realized in the healing ministry. Faint, thematic.
